title: While America Fights Its Data Centers, India Is Rolling Out the Red Carpet. The Numbers Are Staggering.
excerpt: Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon are pouring tens of billions into Indian data centers. Zero taxes until 2047, no public hearings, and tenfold capacity growth projected over the next decade.
body:
American communities are going to war over data centers. Town halls are packed. Zoning boards are under siege. From Virginia to Arizona, residents are fighting to keep the server farms that power the AI revolution out of their backyards.

India is doing the opposite. And it is working.

A Barron's investigation published Thursday reveals the widening gap between how the world's two largest democracies are handling the data-center gold rush. While U.S. municipalities battle over water use, electricity costs, and noise, India is fast-tracking approvals without public hearings, offering cheaper land, and granting tax breaks that extend all the way to 2047 — the centenary of Indian independence.

The result: India is now one of the fastest-growing data-center markets on the planet. Nomura estimates that the country's capacity will grow tenfold over the next decade. Synergy Research Group projects India will account for 3 percent of global data-center capacity within five years, up from 1.3 percent today.

"That may not sound like a big shift, but these are percentages of enormous numbers," said John Dinsdale, Synergy's chief analyst.

## The Numbers Behind the Boom

The investment commitments are staggering. Microsoft has pledged $17.5 billion in India — its largest-ever bet in Asia. Google parent Alphabet is pouring $15 billion into three data-center campuses in Visakhapatnam, a coastal city in Andhra Pradesh. Meta, Amazon, and OpenAI are also adding capacity.

On Thursday, a consortium led by Microsoft and Singapore-based Lightstorm announced the I-2SEA undersea cable, a 3,600-kilometre fibre link connecting India to Malaysia and Singapore. The cable, with landing stations in Machilipatnam — the same Andhra Pradesh region where Meta and Google are building — is expected to go live by late 2029.

India's operational data-center capacity currently stands at about 1.4 gigawatts. Macquarie estimates it could double by 2027 and grow fivefold by 2030 if planned projects are fast-tracked. On the hardware side, Micromax and Taiwan's Phison Electronics have launched MiPhi Semiconductors, a joint venture manufacturing enterprise-grade SSDs in India to serve AI servers and hyperscale data centres — targeting the $270 billion global NAND memory market.

## Why India?

Two forces are converging. First, latency: data centers must be close to their users to reduce lag, and India has the scale to justify the investment. Indians are the second-largest user base for ChatGPT and Claude globally.

Second, policy. In February, India declared zero taxes until 2047 on overseas services by foreign companies that operate data centres in the country. State governments are layering on their own incentives, offering subsidised power rates and expedited land acquisition. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has personally courted the hyperscalers. "Work with India and deliver for all," he told an AI summit in June.

There is no equivalent of the American backlash. Data-center projects in India are approved without public hearings, a contrast that Barron's describes as both an advantage and a source of concern for governance advocates.

## The American Contrast

In the United States, the data-center backlash is intensifying at a sensitive moment. Morgan Stanley estimates that hyperscalers will spend $800 billion on capital expenditure in 2026 alone. OpenAI and Anthropic have both filed confidentially for IPOs. Microsoft, Google, and CoreWeave say they are capacity-constrained.

But community resistance is real. Residents worry about electricity bills, water consumption, and noise. Some municipalities have won moratoriums; others have lost fights and watched construction begin.

The Semiconductor Industry Association estimates that $4 trillion in data-center infrastructure spending is coming through 2028. The question is no longer whether the buildout will happen — it is where.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

The story is deeply personal for Indian-Americans in tech. Many work at the very companies — Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon — that are now investing billions in their home country. India's rise as a data-center hub creates jobs, deepens the technology partnership between the two countries, and diversifies the global AI supply chain away from its current concentration in the American heartland and Northern Virginia.

For diaspora investors, the infrastructure play is becoming hard to ignore. Lightstorm, which connects 19 AI and cloud zones across India through terrestrial fibre, plans to list in India in mid-2027 at a reported valuation of up to $1.5 billion. The ripple effects — from commercial real estate to power infrastructure to semiconductor manufacturing — are only beginning.
